items.title: Louis Armstrong Interview, 1960-08-23
items.q: you wouldn't change your style for that Bob slap to people today play just the same way

ctx.x: Mr. Armstrong you have been in the field for so many years now would you say you have changed your way of

playing say no never change nothing you don't have to change I was taught but one way to play right and good you know what else you gonna do you know you wouldn't change your style for that Bob slap to people today play just the same way so a lot of them do Jackie and James I take on you yeah I think it's a matter of sincerity if you're playing what you believe and you're expressing yourself that they had on that's it I mean if you're going to be a dilettante and try to copy someone or play what you think is…
never come back to me in the jam session do you play with your friends just for fun exactly the same

items.title: Bob Haggart interviewed by Michael Woods, Clinton, New York, September 22, 1995
items.q: Like all Louis Armstrong’s early records. I could sing every note right now... These were all names that I had every one of their records

ctx.x: How did playing bass in those ensembles, how did it give you an education that perhaps you don’t get in a university now?

Well I think they had, they ask the question, how do you learn how to do that? Well I found it’s mostly from listening. You have to have it up here. You have to want to do it. And by listening to records, and listening to other players or groups live, in those days we listened to records all the time. So you’d memorize, you’d hear a guy play a chorus, and you’d play it over so many times you knew it note for note, you could sing it. Like all Louis Armstrong’s early records. I could sing every note right now. You…
Do you think that sometimes even between the bass and the drums that the drummer actually wants you to take the time?
